title: OODA loop interview
about: Questions about how one person observes, orients, decides and acts (John Boyd's OODA loop). Each answer becomes one passage of a corpus.

stages.label: Observe
stages.about: What you take in: where your information comes from, what you notice and what you miss.

questions.text: When you walk into a situation you don't know yet, what do you notice first, and why that?
What sources of information do you trust most, and what makes you trust them?
Which sources do you distrust or ignore, and what led you to that?
How do you know when something around you has changed?
What early signs tell you a situation is about to go well?
What early signs tell you a situation is about to go badly?
What do you tend to miss that other people catch?
What do you catch that other people tend to miss?
When you are tired, stressed or rushed, what happens to what you notice?
How much do you rely on what you see and hear yourself, and how much on what others tell you? What decides the balance?
When two sources tell you opposite things, what do you do?
How do you go looking for information you don't have yet? Describe a recent example.
What makes you stop gathering information and feel you have enough?
What kinds of information do you deliberately avoid, and what does avoiding them do for you?
How do you notice what other people are feeling or intending?
What part do numbers, data or measurements play in what you notice?
What part does your body (gut feelings, tension, energy) play in what you notice?
Which people do you watch most closely, and what are you watching for?
When something surprises you, what do you do in the next few minutes?
Think of a time you missed an important signal. What made you miss it?
What do you check routinely, every day or every week, and why those things?
How does your mood change what you pay attention to?
How do you tell a real signal from noise?
What information reaches you too late, and what does that cost you?
How do you notice your own mistakes?
If you could add one source of information to your life, what would it be and what would it change?

stages.label: Orient
stages.about: How you make sense of it: the experience, beliefs, values and habits of mind that turn what you notice into a picture.

questions.text: When you take in something new, what do you compare it to first?
Which experiences most shaped how you read situations today, and how?
Which people, books or traditions taught you how to think about the world?
What do you believe about people that guides how you interpret what they do?
What do you believe about how the world works that most people around you don't?
What do you hold most important, and how does it color what you see?
How does where you come from (family, culture, place) shape how you make sense of things?
How do your current goals change how you interpret what is happening?
When a situation is ambiguous, which interpretation do you tend to reach for first, and why?
What are your usual explanations for why things go wrong?
What are your usual explanations for why things go right?
How do you find out that your picture of a situation is wrong?
Describe a time you changed your mind about something important. What changed it?
What would it take to change your mind about something you now feel sure of?
Which of your assumptions do you rarely question?
Which of your biases do you know about, and how do they show up?
How do you weigh your intuition against careful reasoning?
How do you make sense of a person whose behaviour surprises you?
When you face something entirely new, how do you build a picture of it?
What patterns do you see repeating in your life, and what do you think drives them?
How do your emotions shape how you interpret events?
Whose way of seeing things do you borrow when your own isn't enough?
What do you think causes success in the things you care about?
What do you think causes failure in those things?
How do you judge what matters most in a situation and what can be ignored?
What makes something feel dangerous or safe to you?
What makes something feel urgent, or able to wait?
How would someone who sees the world very differently describe your blind spots?

stages.label: Decide
stages.about: How you choose: the options you consider, how you weigh them and when you commit.

questions.text: Describe how you made an important decision recently, step by step.
How do you know when it is time to decide rather than keep thinking?
How many options do you usually consider, and where do they come from?
What makes one option stand out over the others?
What do you do when every option looks bad?
What do you do when two options look equally good?
Which rules, principles or habits do you rely on to decide, and what do they do for you?
Which decisions do you make quickly, and which slowly? What makes the difference?
Who do you consult before deciding, and what do you want from them?
When do you decide alone, and why?
How do you weigh what you might gain against what you might lose?
How do you weigh the short term against the long term?
How do your values rule some options out before you consider them?
What part does fear play in your decisions?
What part do hope and excitement play?
How do you decide under pressure, when there is no time to think?
How do you decide when key information is missing?
What kinds of decisions do you put off, and what happens when you do?
When have you decided too quickly, and what led to it?
When have you decided too slowly, and what led to it?
How do you judge whether a decision was a good one, apart from how it turned out?
Which decision are you proudest of, and what made it good?
Which decision do you regret most, and what would you do differently?
How do other people's expectations shape what you choose?
How do you decide what not to do?
Once a decision is made but before you act on it, do you revisit it? What makes you reopen it?

stages.label: Act
stages.about: How you carry it out, and how the results come back to what you notice next.

questions.text: Once you have decided, how quickly do you act, and what speeds you up or slows you down?
What gets in the way between deciding and doing?
How do you choose the first step of an action?
How do you act when you are not sure it will work?
How do you get other people to act with you?
What do you do when an action goes differently than you expected?
When do you stop or reverse something you have started?
How do you keep going when acting gets hard or dull?
Which habits or routines carry out much of what you do without a decision, and where did they come from?
Which actions do you put the most care into, and why?
How do you act differently when others are watching?
Which limits (time, money, energy, people) most shape what you can do, and how do you work around them?
How do you tell whether an action worked?
After acting, what do you look at first?
How quickly do you learn from the results of what you did, and how?
Describe a time something you did changed how you saw the situation.
How does what you did yesterday shape what you notice today?
When something you did fails, what do you change first: what you watch, how you read it, how you decide, or how you act?
Where in your life do you move faster than the people or situations around you, and where slower? What makes the difference?
What makes you take the initiative rather than respond to others?
How do you act when you need to surprise or outmanoeuvre someone?
How do you react when someone else moves faster than you?
Do you try to make your actions hard for others to predict? How, and why?
What would you do differently if you had to act twice as fast?
What would you do differently if you had all the time you needed?
If you could change one thing about how you get from seeing to doing, what would it be?
